entry.title: NBA 2026-27 Standings Predictions
entry.content:
On the eve of what is slated to be the NBA’s most exciting regular season to date, how do I forecast the teams to finish when all is said and done?
For the first time in a long time, the Eastern Conference projects to be stronger than the West, with LeBron James and Kawhi Leonard heading east, and Giannis Antetokounmpo and Jaylen Brown joining forces with budding superteams.
Will the Knicks experience a championship hangover? Should we doubt the Nuggets as a playoff lock? Which team(s) will surprise us all and take the NBA by storm as the Spurs did last season?
Find out now in my NBA 2026-27 Regular Season standings predictions, with nuanced modeling for off-season moves, roster continuity, team identity, and injury luck.

Western Conference


1. San Antonio Spurs [Last Season: 2 seed, 62-20]

Of course, the Spurs’ success rides on the shoulders of their 7’4 giant, Victor Wembanyama. Posting the 4th best offense and 3rd best defense last season, with fantastic continuity and a clear identity, the Spurs will have another immensely successful season if Wemby can stay healthy. This team is young, always developing, always feisty, and their frontcourt depth has been strongly bolstered through their off-season moves. The franchise has a clear intent to put physicality around Wemby, raising their floor, and Dylan Harper’s seemingly endless potential gives me optimism for a high ceiling. Although each team in the Southwestern Conference should be improved from last year, potentially stealing a few more wins from the Spurs (last year they went 13-3 against division rivals), I think the talent and system here is too great to ultimately deny their top spot in the West.

Notable Departures A+

  • None... yet.

Notable Additions A−

  • Tobias Harris provides a super reliable veteran presence on both ends of the court. Quaintance and Reed Jr. add significant depth at the four/big-man position.

Roster Continuity A+

  • Kept their most important players: Wemby, Fox, Castle, Harper, Champagnie, Johnson, Barnes, Bryant, and Kornet.
  • Lost Olynyk, Sochan, and Biyombo, but these aren't particularly notable departures. Overall, excellent roster continuity.

System & Coaching A+

  • It's easy to win games when you have a 7'4" defensive demigod breaking out as a potential future GOAT candidate. The Wemby-centric system features feisty role players who create disruptions on both ends of the court.
  • Mitch Johnson (CBS Rank: 9) had some potential missteps in last season's playoffs, but winning so many games without Wemby during the regular season gives me confidence that he can correct those mistakes in just his second year in charge.

Injury Projection C

  • Tobias Harris suffered a calf strain during training camp that may keep him out of the season opener. Hopefully, this doesn't linger into the regular season.
  • Quaintance may not join the team on the court until midseason, even under an optimistic projection.
  • One would expect their great injury luck last season to regress toward the mean, potentially creating more challenges than they experienced last year.

External Projections

ESPN BPI Rank #2
DraftKings Win Total Line 60.5


2. Oklahoma City Thunder [Last Season: 1 seed, 64-18]

Trust me, I do feel guilty putting one of the youngest teams, who were on pace to break the regular season wins record last season until injuries held them back (and still conquered the league with the best record in the NBA anyways) in the 2nd Seed position. They have the two-time reigning MVP, got back all-star Jalen Williams, and one could reasonably project ever greater development from Cason Wallace, Chet Holmgren, and Jared McCain. This roster is feisty, incredibly well-balanced, has a clear identity and fantastic coaching, and absolutely no one would be surprised if they hit on their draft selections again. Name one weakness they have. No matter the opponent, they should rightly feel they would win on any given night. That being said, they did lose a number of winning players to shed salary they spent on Isaiah Hartenstein in the form of Lu Dort, Isaiah Joe, and Aaron Wiggins. This, and my belief in Wembanyama as a transcendent NBA talent are the only two reasons I’ll give the razor-thin margin in favor of the Spurs as a bold prediction.

Notable Departures C-

  • Lu Dort
  • Isaiah Joe
  • Aaron Wiggins

Notable Additions B

  • Jared McCain only played 30 games last season due to being traded halfway through the season. I expect a much bigger role from him.
  • Nikola Topić only played 10 games last season after undergoing testicular surgery and chemotherapy. I expect a much bigger role from him. (Edit: Topić has been dealing with a back issue that's keeping him out indefinitely as the season starts... not what anyone wants to hear.)
  • Aday Mara and Bennett Stirtz could both potentially be ready-to-go impactors in defined roles, but I wouldn’t expect them to rise up to record-changing players immediately. Having Thomas Sorber this season for depth could be a strong swing factor, though. (Edit: Sorber is out indefinitely to start the season as he recovers from a minor knee surgery).

Roster Continuity B

  • Kept their most key players (Shai, JDub, Chet, Caruso, Cason, Hartenstein, McCain). Having Ajay Mitchell, Jaylin Williams, and Kenrich Williams return is nice. Lost some key contributors who played tons of minutes including Dort, Joe, and Wiggins.

System & Coaching A+

  • Very well defined around star players and defensive/transition ecosystem where role players know exactly how to create positive impact. I trust Mark Dagineault (CBS Rank 2) a lot.

Injury Projection A-

  • Isaiah Hartenstein only played 47 games last season due to calf/lower leg injury, but the Thunder shedded multiple important contracts this offseason to keep him for another 3 years, clearly investing in his interior physicality, reliable offensive and defensive presence, and ability to act as a glue guy.
  • JDub only played 33 games last season due to wrist and hamstring injuries last year, I’d project he plays a lot more this year which should help a lot.
  • Overall, last season they were quite unlucky with injuries last season as many projections had them winning 73+ games at the start of the year. A return to average would mean they experience more luck but there are some lingering doubts with Topić and Sorber out to start the year.

External Projections

ESPN BPI Rank #1
DraftKings Win Total Line 62.5


3. Los Angeles Lakers [Last Season: 4 seed, 53-29]

Welcome to the Luka show. The Lakers have transitioned off of the LeBron James era and rapidly constructed a Luka-centric roster. Walker Kessler is a drastic improvement on what the Lakers were rolling out last season as he should provide fantastic rim protection on defense and all-time scoring efficiency offensively. Although this looks like a completely new roster, they are bringing in a ton of defensive-minded, win-now, experienced NBA players which raises their floor. The offense is not the side to worry about. Building an effective defense around Luka and Austin Reaves is quite the challenge, but JJ Redick seems to be up to the task as he hopes to instill consistent defensive intensity and discipline.


4. Houston Rockets [Last Season: 5 seed, 52-30]

The Rockets have desperately needed a reliable point guard as Reed Sheppard simply needs more time to develop. Adding Fred VanVleet’s 3-point shooting and steady playmaking will be a great relief for everyone on this team. I am mostly optimistic that the Rockets will have a great season, although I would bet we can’t expect 38 year old Kevin Durant to play 78 games again this year. Yes, the Rockets lose some relevant depth, but their strong off-season and overall continuity should be enough for this team to maintain their success from last year.


5. Denver Nuggets [Last Season: 3 seed, 54-28]

Another season, another round of disappointment from the Nuggets front office. What’s new? The Nuggets scraped into the 3 seed last year due to the force of all-star Jamal Murray and Peyton Watson carrying the team during injuries to Nikola Jokić and Aaron Gordon, and a late winning streak against tanking teams. Although the starting lineup has reached outstanding success, able to battle anyone on their day, another year older means we can continue to expect injury misfortune to hold them back. The Nuggets desperately needed 3-point shooting and DEFENSE. none of which was addressed in their off season moves. I hope Alpha Diallo translates well and becomes an NBA defensive stalwart. I like DeMar as a steady offensive option off the bench, I’ll let myself be pleasantly surprised by Tyus, Marvin, and Lonnie, and I think Trevon Brazile projects as a dynamic, athletically imposing future option with enough time to develop an NBA game. Ultimately, the Nuggets possess a core on the tail end of excellence and retooling around Jokić may be necessary if they want to reach the peaks they did in 2023 (especially if they want to beat the TWolves in the playoffs).


6. Minnesota Timberwolves [Last Season: 6 seed, 49-33]

The Timberwolves took a big swing trading away Julius Randle, Naz Reid, an unprotected first-round pick and 3 second-round picks for all-star Lamelo Ball. Lamelo provides clear value to the Twolves as one of the most talented offensive engines in the league, commandeering playmaking duties from Anthony Edwards as he’s been wishing for so long. Although the Lamelo + Ant combination is perfect on paper, likely the best backcourt in the league, I expect they will show elite flashes of success throughout the year, but only translate that to win dominance later in the season. It takes time to merge two star guards, especially if they’re both as high usage as these two (both >30%, top 17 in the league last year). I like the flier on Kuminga, but I doubt he alone will be enough to bolster the physicality and size that was crucial to their identity last year.


7. Dallas Mavericks [Last Season: 12 seed, 26-56]

Most NBA 2026-27 standings predictions seemingly take a swing on the Mavericks, Grizzlies, or Jazz to be much improved from last season. My bet is on the Mavs. I personally am very excited for first time NBA coach Dusty May (CBS Rank 26) who was amazing in college and I think he’s going to bring a fresh, analytically driven approach to this team. Yes, the roster has Masai Ujiri’s fingerprint all over it with an overabundance of unspecialized tall wings, and there are reasons to seriously doubt its 3 point shooting and ball handling depth as a result, but I think Cooper Flagg will truly break out as a star, finishing the season with serious all-NBA consideration.

Notable Departures C-

  • Klay Thompson
  • Ryan Nembhard
  • Brandon Williams

Notable Additions A−

  • Kyrie Irving, played 0 games for them last year rehabbing from ACL tear late in the 2024-25 season
  • Santi Aldama
  • Zaccharie Risacher
  • Marcus Sasser
  • Morez Johnson Jr

Roster Continuity B+

  • The mavs keep the majority of their key contributors and depth, although there are a few notable changes, the replacements should slide right in without too much adjustment.

System & Coaching A+

  • Dusty May (CBS Rank 26) is a new head coach, but will bring a solid, uniting personality to the team and an analytically driven offense centered on foundational principles.

Injury Projection A

  • The Mavs were average to somewhat unlucky last season with injuries. Besides Dereck Lively II, there’s no reason to believe they would become very unlucky this season, so injury factor shouldn’t play a huge role outside of Kyrie’s reintroduction.

External Projections

ESPN BPI Rank #22
DraftKings Win Total Line 33.5


8. Phoenix Suns [Last Season: 8 seed, 45-37]

Last season was somewhat of a breakout year for the Suns, finishing in 8th with Devin Booker only playing 64 games, Dillon Brooks and Grayson Allen playing 56 and 51 respectively, and Jalen Green playing only 32 games. The Suns can reasonably expect another solid campaign with a nice mix of steady veterans and high-upside young players, but they’re no longer the surprise team in the West anymore. I think contention to avoid the play-in is too tough and the Suns will end up in a similar spot to last year.


9. Portland Trail Blazers [Last Season: 7 seed, 42-40]

The Trailblazers were a surprise team last season to some (personally, I was more optimistic than most) owing to the breakout of Deni Avdija and defensive consistency from Toumani Camara and Donovan Clingan. Clearly, there will be a huge shakeup with the addition of two time all-star Ja Morant and similarly high-usage Damian Lillard. Starting both of those offensive-minded, small guards puts heavy pressure on that defense which was 14th in DRTG last season. With the reintroduction of their franchise legend alongside a host of young players to develop, there’s a lot for first time head coach Micah Nori to figure out rotation-wise. Although, I see talent and creativity giving this roster another surprising, competitive edge to unsuspecting teams.


10. New Orleans Pelicans [Last Season: 11 seed, 26-56]

The Pelicans are routinely one of the hardest franchises to be optimistic about. That being said, I am willing to stick my neck out a bit for them this year with the expectation that Dejounte Murray, who should raise their floor, is healthy this season. Of course, you cannot bet on the Pelicans avoiding injury as they have been arguably the most cursed team in recent history. Yes, Zion might not play 62 games this year like he did last season, and yes his fit with burgeoning Derik Queen does seem clunky, but there’s still an overwhelming amount of young talent in this locker room. To me, Jamahl Mosley will play the role of a potter and if he’s able to shape the team into connected cohesion, I believe the Pelicans are a team who finally deserve some good luck.


11. Utah Jazz [Last Season: 15 Seed, 22-60]

Many feel highly optimistic about this Jazz roster who threw in the towel early last season, obscuring their real potential. They made fantastic acquisitions in the form of former defensive player of the year and two-time all-star Jaren Jackson Jr., drafting Darryn Peterson who projects as a generational talent, and recouping some NBA experience through trades. Will Hardy is one of the best coaches in the league, and I’m a massive Keyonte George fan, although I have serious doubts about this defense. They may catch lightning in a bottle on certain nights, but I don’t believe they will have the consistency necessary for regular season wins.


12. Memphis Grizzlies [Last Season: 13 seed, 25-57]

A lot of optimism surrounds this young Grizzlies team which has drafted extremely well over the last few years. They’ve struck gold on underrated talents out of nowhere, and I think their off-season additions are quietly among the best in the league. Cameron Boozer may well come in looking like a vet, and sweep up the rookie of the year award as he should form a formidable duo with Zach Edey in the frontcourt. Feisty guard play and physically imposing backcourt depth is a winning formula at the very top of the Western Conference, although this team needs a generational star to get there. Even if it’s too early for this talent to equate to wins just yet, fans should be excited about their leap into a new, promising direction.


13. Golden State Warriors [Last Season: 10 Seed, 37-45]

This roster was extremely mid last year, and I’m honestly surprised they got as far as they did with Steph only playing 43 games. Doubling down on this old roster by drafting a 24 year-old win-now rookie when they only clinched the 10 seed last season is quite the decision, one that I don’t think will pay off for them long term. They’ve clearly embraced the Walt Disney adage “growing old is mandatory, but growing up is optional!” The dubs are desperately hoping for more health this season, although they’re not likely to experience it with Curry barely recovering from a right ankle sprain in a pre-season practice, Porzingis currently listed as out indefinitely, and Jimmy Butler likely to be out until February 2027. If Yaxel is a revelation and Steph Curry can play respectable time on the court, this team may not be one of the worst in the league… hopefully.


14. Los Angeles Clippers [Last Season: 9 Seed, 42-40]

Having to perform intense mental gymnastics to figure out how this team can defend anything is not a positive omen for your season. Another year older, and with high injury risk to key players (eg. Garland, Ingram), I struggle to find real optimism for the Clippers to convert individual flashes into regular season team success this year. Not being fully in control of their own first round picks from now through 2033 means this team has a lot of strategy to plan out. Let’s hope Keaton Wagler shows he can be a star in this league.


15. Sacramento Kings [Last Season: 14 seed, 22-60]

Worse than a bottom 25 team offensively and defensively last season, the Kings are looking for any sign of optimism going into their 2026-27 campaign. I project them as a team hoping to give high playing time to young players like center Maxime Raynaud and wing Nique Clifford, while brainstorming solutions to exchange their veteran assets for a clearer franchise direction. I’m just about the biggest Darius Acuff Jr. fan besides his mom, so I’m really looking forward to watching him and other 2026 draftees Emanuel Sharp and Alex Karaban. Kings, you may lose a lot, but keep your head up lest you let your crown fall.

Eastern Conference


1. Boston Celtics [Last Season: 2 Seed, 56-26]

It’s well established that Joe Mazzulla and his Celtics roster are regular season juggernauts. With a clear team identity, fantastic continuity, and the addition of all-NBA First Team mainstay Jayson Tatum back into the lineup, I think the Celtics have the right concoction to rise to the top of this very competitive Eastern Conference. Some view the Jalen Brown trade for Paul George as a massive downgrade, yet I see the value in viewing this effectively as a trade for Tatum with PG13 as a potentially elite bonus. Mitchell Robinson is the off-season’s most underrated acquisition as an impact player– regardless of what his playing time looks like, he provides great value as a dominating rebounding presence on this 3-point shooting happy team. Nothing is given, but this roster should know that better than most.


2. New York Knicks [Last Season: 3 Seed, 53-29]

Coming off of a dominant playoffs en route to their first NBA Championship in 53 years, many consider the Knicks as a shoe-in for the 1 seed. I am conserving some gusto on this front, noting that Mitchell Robinson played a huge role for their success, and projecting a bit of a “championship hangover” for a roster that has relied heavily on high starter minutes over the last few years. Not much has changed in the lineup, so we can expect the Knicks to continue to put themselves in tough situations game-to-game, regularly requiring large comebacks and the ability to elevate in the clutch. They’ll still be great. They’re still a team to fear in the postseason.


3. Cleveland Cavaliers [Last Season: 4 Seed, 52-30]

The Cavs run it back, completely sure that they just need to find the right wing to harmonize their elite guard duo with their elite frontcourt duo. I’d give it a 50% chance Peyton Watson is that wing, positioned well to break out with established defensive covering and flashes of explosive two-way potential to fulfill the Cavs’ hopes and dreams. The Cavs are a funny team as they’ve experienced an abundance of clear success in the last few years, yet this regularity has caused them to be overlooked in some ways. Kenny Atkinson may not fully understand how analytics works, but I would blindly put my faith in his formula for regular season wins nonetheless.


4. Detroit Pistons [Last Season: 1 Seed, 60-22]

Since when was projecting the second youngest (weighted average by minutes played last season) team, who also dominated the conference winning 4 more games than the second seed, to now be a top 4 seed a hot take? In my opinion, many analysts are overreacting to the summer Duren drama and the infusion of talent into top Eastern Conference teams by plummeting the Pistons down the standings. Yes, they lost some frontcourt depth which helped them embrace their physically bruising identity last season, but I like their moves around the margin and I feel fine expecting their young core to continue impressing. Cade, bring home that MVP for my fantasy team.


5. Philadelphia 76ers [Last Season: 7 Seed, 45-37]

Welcome to the show, Jalen Brown and LeBron James! Projecting the 76ers regular season success feels like a departure into madness as they boast the league’s most talented starting 5 on paper, yet feel destined for injury misfortune. The overwhelming talent and respectable depth should be enough for this team to find success all season, although I find a top seed prediction too risky in this Eastern Conference bloodbath. They care more that everyone will be healthy for the playoffs, anyhow. What feels more likely is that this team will host the most storylines throughout the season… I can’t wait to watch them hoop!


6. Indiana Pacers [Last Season: 14 Seed, 19-63]

I hear you that a 14th seed swinging right back up to a 6th seed sounds optimistic. But, I believe in the magic and offensive identity that Tyrese Haliburton adds to this Pacers roster, expecting a huge turnaround from their 29th ranked offense last season. Maybe it’s blind faith, but I like this team’s continuity, elite coaching, and vast potential for any young player to break out out of nowhere. Zubac is a perfect fit for this roster with sneaky experience. It will be interesting to finally see how this Pacers rendition will perform with some real expectations going into the start of the season.


7. Toronto Raptors [Last Season: 5 Seed, 46-36]

Adding Kawhi Leonard to this previously underrated roster may be a concoction for him to form the best duo in the league alongside star Scottie Barnes. Already a top 5 defense, adding the steady release valve of Kawhi’s effortless bucket-getting to this top 15 offense should mean this is a team of assassins. In the event of injury misfortune, a rational prediction given Kawhi’s history, they are rolling the dice that their young depth can step up to the challenge, which makes me a little hesitant to put them too high in the standings. Losing Mamu is tough, but they still have an ace in head coach Darko Rajakovic. You can tell my head is spinning on where exactly they’ll fall when all is said and done.


8. Miami Heat [Last Season: 10 Seed, 43-39]

Giannis Antetokounmpo, referred to as the “Greek Freak” is an unstoppable force, statline dominating, absolutely winning player. Adding a top ~5 player like him to a consistently respectable roster with the best coach in the league spells horror for the rest of the Eastern Conference. That being said, the Heat did give up a lot to get him, something the Nets or Suns (not a sneak diss, KD, please don’t @ me) or Bucks or Sixers could tell you does not guarantee immediate success. The Heat should stand as an authoritative force on defense, with only above-average to all-time defenders across their starting five. Unfortunately, the modern NBA requires offense and specifically reliable 3-point production to excel in the win column. Giannis may average 30 points per game again, and we may casually anticipate the random 83 point scoring outburst from Bam Adebayo, but I retain my doubts that the Heat will regularly produce enough offense to win regularly in close finishes. (PS, I respect both of you, Klay and Timmy, and would be absolutely delighted to watch you guys rip nets all season).


9. Atlanta Hawks [Last Season: 6 Seed, 46-36]

I’m very excited to see the Hawks’ first full season under the stewardship of breakout star Jalen Johnson. With a multitude of promising young talent to build off of the base provided by fantastic off-season acquisitions in the form of ever-reliable role players Aaron Wiggins, Lu Dort, and Dorian Finney-Smith, there’s a chance this team catches flight (I’m so sorry) and breaks into Tier 1. The Hawks were a team looking for short term stability given small injury misfortune and the undertaking of finding their way in the post-Trae Young era last season, so I believe there should only be room for good vibes in the locker room this year. My projected drop in their seed this year is a pure reflection of the influx of off-season success in other Eastern Conference teams. Optimistically, this means with good luck the Hawks will have a real opening to deliver blows to higher seeded injury-riddled teams in the playoffs. NAW, you may not be known by the average human, but you’re a star to me.


10. Orlando Magic [Last Season: 8 Seed, 45-37]

Although it feels like we’re many years into this project, Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner are still young. I view them as very consistent players when healthy, and the roster has not experienced essentially any overturn, so we should logically anticipate a very similar looking season to last year. That is, until you realize the East got better across the board, notably including a few of their Southeastern Division rivals they have to play multiple times this year. Even if the Magic finally experience a fully healthy season for their starters, I question if it’s enough to make noise in the East. I’m not naïve enough to predict the Magic will finally figure out an effective offense with the same exact cast just because they have a new head coach. Although, their respectable defense and consistent pulse should equate to enough regular season wins to avoid irrelevancy.


11. Charlotte Hornets [Last Season: 9 Seed, 44-38]

It’s no mystery to me why Charlotte experienced their most magical, successful season in a long time during Lamelo Ball’s healthiest campaign since his sophomore, all-star rendition. Orbiting around Lamelo’s offensive gravity, many young and auxiliary players stepped up in their roles netting the Hornets a top 5 offense and top 11 defense in 2025-26. There would be absolutely no reason to get cold feet on this fresh roster + coach matrimony unless the Hornets completely doubt Lamelo will ever be this healthy again. What sounds like a negative summary has more than just a silver lining. I love the way young players Kon Knueppel, Moussa Diabaté, Ryan Kalkbrenner, and Sion James stepped up last year, and I’m starting to gain real trust in their drafting savvy now seeing them select Christian Anderson Jr. and Hannes Steinbach– both of whom are awesome, by the way. Naz Reid is a fan favorite, and the other experience they’ve brought in should hold them in a somewhat competitive position. Ultimately, trading your superstar for only role players will enact regression in the short term, and this roster needs time before it produces magic again.


12. Washington Wizards [Last Season: 15 Seed, 17-65]

I too am buying into the hype that adding floor raisers Trae Young and Anthony Davis will instantly improve a young roster. Wouldn’t it be nice if the Washington Wizards became a team to finally possess some cause for belief? They have an overabundance of young potential, and I think the start of this campaign will be paramount to the crucial near-term decisions they need to make. This roster may look different yet again by the end of this year or next, but I have faith that if they make intelligent decisions regarding how to best build around AJ Dybantsa’s superstar potential, they may eventually become a fearsome squad. Head coach Brian Keefe will be on the hot seat if the Wizards fail to eclipse 20 regular season wins for the fourth-straight season. Don’t let me down.


13. Chicago Bulls [Last Season: 12 Seed, 31-51]

The franchise that has truly experienced it all. Untouchable in the 90’s, unlucky in the early 2010’s, unrelentingly mid in the early 2020’s, and now– at long last– just plain old bad. The Bulls waited too long to blow things up, as new draft lottery rules now mean they need to win just enough games to get a higher chance at a top pick. I like the additions of Norman Powell, Nic Claxton, and Buddy Hield for this reason. Matas Buzelis and Caleb Wilson will both take awhile to fully develop anyways, so why not add a few non-invasive vets? With the cleanest near-future draft portfolio, owning all of their own 1st- and 2nd-round round picks over the next 7 years, the Bulls are in a surprisingly comfy spot. Just hold on, find which playstyles and player archetypes jive well together, and plan a tactical strike when the team has a chance to compete. Definitely don’t rush into something stupid.


14. Brooklyn Nets [Last Season: 13 Seed, 20-62]

The Nets can no longer be considered the younger, less handsome brother of the New York Knicks. With what happened in the 2025-26 season, they have been pushed so far into the Knicks’ shadow they may as well fully embrace the dark side. I’d actually like it if the new demotion zone this year meant we could let Jordi Fernández draft his own team of players and give them a shot. If there’s a silver lining to this season, it’s that the Nets have an incredible haul of upcoming first round draft picks. Although this current front office’s draft selections seem to have only misses like a NAV album, I will give the young guys the grace of time to find their way. There’s a real chance Mikel Brown and Egor Dëmin could produce sparks in the dark if they find their rhythm.


15. Milwaukee Bucks [Last Season: 11 Seed, 32-50]

Despite their players currently looking like a Love Island cast, the Bucks did not have a long, hot summer. Actually, they decided with haste that a 32 win season was too balmy for their northern tastes and quickly traded franchise hero Giannis Antetokounmpo for, well, a Herro of some sort. To those who haven’t yet taken a deep dive into this roster’s contents, it might sound a tad mean to say the Bucks will have to scrap and fight every game they can to not be one of the worst three teams in the league. Oh wait, they don’t even own their own first round draft pick this year (nor in 2029). So, wins to them are like volleyballs to a castaway: rarely encountered and largely unhelpful anyhow. Brayden Burries should have a long and impactful NBA career, ideally for a more inspiring team, so if you guys could trade him when the Gary Tent inquisition leaves you desperate that’d be great, thanks. Winter is coming.

entry.title: March Madness Tournament Predictor
entry.content:
Heart Versus Algorithm: An Analytical Approach to Filling out my March Madness Bracket

Eric Rumsfeld
May 1st, 2026

For the 2026 NCAA D1’s Men’s Tournament, also known as March Madness, I built two brackets: one from instinct, and one from a machine learning (ML) model. Only one of them finished in the 99.4th percentile.

One Bracket from the Heart

Created March 15th, 2026.

Heading into Selection Sunday for this year’s March Madness Tournament, I had already decided who my champion was going to be. The Arizona Wildcats. I knew they were a team with a plan, and a team who was going to execute that plan relentlessly until they saw their colors streaming down as confetti in April. I was confident that I could pick the winner of the tournament based on vibes because I had done it previously with Baylor in 2021, UConn in 2024, and Florida in 2025. By tournament time, the Wildcats just went on a hot streak, winning some important games against Top-25-ish ranked teams like BYU, Houston, Kansas, Iowa State, as well as the Big 12 Tournament Championship. I knew they had momentum, and they knew their own strengths better than any other team. After Selection Sunday, I crafted my bracket with picks from the heart, and labeled it, ironically:

  Eric’s Golden Mean.

And One Bracket from a Forest

Created March 18th, 2026.

I built an ML algorithm called a random forest to predict the outcome of games in the March Madness Tournament. To make a long story short, I bought a Yaxel Lendeborg Michigan jersey later that day. My second bracket, with picks originating solely from the ML model, was named:

  Eric’s Evil Eye.


This article will describe how, although your human eyes may be deceived sometimes, the proof of success lies in the numbers, and a careful coding approach can lead to some strongly predictive performances.

My Unique Data Approach

Leading into the tournament, an idea kept banging around my head to train a machine learning model solely on college basketball teams’ relative strengths, instead of just their raw counting numbers. College basketball is a unique realm where stylistic matchup hunting and exposing relative weaknesses seem to matter so much in high pressure games that can be swung in just a few runs.

In fact, seeking relative advantages is important at any level of basketball. Even from a young age, a player will hear a coach say “he can’t dribble with his left so send him that way,” or, “she can’t shoot from 3 so sag off and prioritize protecting the paint.”

A great example of this stylistic game determinism is shown in the Cincinnati vs Kansas matchup from February 21st, 2026. Unranked Cincy took down the #8 Jayhawks (who were favored at -520 by DraftKings moneyline1) in what ended up being a dominant style late game after 12 lead changes through the first 30 minutes. Kansas, usually a top-ranked, assertive rebounding team was completely outclassed on the boards, losing the rebound battle 3-13 in the last 10.5 minutes of game time. The offensive boards nabbed by Cincy lead to kick out, wide-open threes, one of their very favorite looks this season. By February, Cincy was attempting 5.2 more 3’s per game, ranking 184 teams ahead of Kansas along this metric. This stylistic advantage paid off as Cincy shot 39% from downtown that game, making 8 more than Kansas (who shot 22%) and securing them a very respectable 84-68 win away from home2.

With this in mind, I knew the stats being fed into my March Madness model had to relate directly to how the two teams on the court stacked up against each other.

My hypothesis was that game outcomes could be predicted if the numbers revealed a team’s strong relative advantage against their opponent.

Data Challenges, Coding Process, and Description of the Model

Data Prep

I obtained the data for this project from two open-access Kaggle resources posted by Jonathan Pilafas3 and Nishaan Amin4. The former contains a wealth of regular season team-level statistics, collected and pooled from other sources like kenpom5, going back to the 2002 season. The latter contains each March Madness Tournament matchup, the seed numbers, and final game scores since 2008.

The main roadblock in carrying out the coding process for this project, as will sound familiar to experienced data scientists, was not actually in training the model itself, but in managing and uniting these two datasets. While one set contained team names like “Connecticut” and “Florida St.”, and the other containing “UConn” and “Florida State”, I knew I had to create some mapping system to marry these two. The planned 2 hours I set aside for this project turned into 10 due to specific, nuanced data challenges like these. In the end, I performed the mapping in Python (the coding language I used for all of this project) as meticulously and thoroughly as humanly possible, ensuring my final dataset could be trusted for analysis.

When I had the master historical dataset with each March Madness matchup, who won, and descriptive stats for each team, I then copied and reversed the pasted dataset, doubling it in size without changing any inherent qualities. Admittedly, this behavior sounds strange on first hearing. However, this is a commonly used tactic to cut down on potential biases the model may accidentally learn6. For example, while I may want the model to learn that the higher seeded team does in fact win a lot in March7, I don’t want it to start believing that the team listed first in the dataset wins a lot of the time just because it is listed first8.

Selecting the Features

But, which data should I care about for my study? I started with my own ball knowledge. To me, scoring, defense, rebounding, shooting efficiency, experience, coaching, and street cred (seed) are important factors when predicting the outcome of a basketball game. I performed investigatory research online and finalized a list of 19 team statistics, such as 3 point percentage, to be fed into my model9. These selected statistics will be called “features” to align with standard machine learning terminology.

The Random Forest Model

When my dataset was satisfactorily prepared, I trained my model using a machine learning tool called a “Random Forest Algorithm”. Given an input dataset, this algorithm creates a series of decision trees to make a prediction about new data. In my case, each decision tree looks at a subset of the data, deciding which feature values may be important for determining the outcome of a game, and casts an official vote as to which team will win. If this model were hypothetically applied to the Kansas vs Cincy game from February, for example, one branch of the tree may look at Kansas’s relative rebounding strength and defensive block percentage over Cincy, and cast a vote for Kansas to win as a result. Meanwhile, a few other trees may have looked at Cincy’s relative standout 3 point field goal rate, and sided with them instead. With many trees voting, the ensemble “forest” creates a final prediction via coded democracy. My model created 500 trees, so if 300 in the forest voted for Kansas, then the result would be a determined 60% probability of them winning:

\(\frac{300}{500} = 0.6\).

With that being done, all I had to do was input all of the first round matchups, and see what the model could cook up!

How Can the Model Be Trusted?

Arguably, the most important aspect of any ML algorithm is knowing that you can rely on its outputs. This model would have no advantages over a random coin toss, much less my own unshakeable eye test, if I didn’t know it’d have some strong predictive accuracy. Digging into the numbers, I segmented some of the master dataset away, calling it the test set, and reserving the bulk of the data to be the training set. I trained my model on the training set, and had it report back to me its predictive accuracy on the test set: 73.93% of the time it called the correct winner. This percentage is right at the forefront of top performing models designed with similar methods. For example, Shen et al. 201610 report a 71% accuracy from their RFA model in their study of the 2015 tournament. I knew the model could be improved yet, so I tuned it with a simple parameter-space search of hyperparameters to achieve the best possible model. This approach boosted my test-set prediction accuracy to 74.76%. Another important check includes the probability distribution plot, which shows how often a confidence interval was assigned to a game outcome. If the model assigns something near a 50% confidence interval to every game outcome, then you may as well save yourself the time and repeatedly flip a coin to fill out your bracket. On the other hand, if the model is close to 100% confident in every pick, you know it can’t be trusted because March Madness games are inherently chaotic, and many come down to last-second shots, or unpredictable human factors. Fig. 1 shows a simple visualization of the probability distribution of first round matchups in the 2026 tournament after one roll of the model. That most confidence levels fall in the 60-80% range is a great sign that this model is well-calibrated.

Results and Implications

Now to the fun part! How did the model perform in this year’s tournament, what spicy picks did it call, and how badly would it have dominated my family’s bracket pool?

Most Confident Predictions

My model was correctly the most confident that the following outcomes would occur:

  • Kansas beats California Baptist — 82.53%
  • Nebraska beats Troy — 80.11%
  • UCLA beats UCF — 78.42%

Games the Model Thought Could Go Either Way

  • Georgia beats Saint Louis — 51.34%11
  • Saint John’s beats Northern Iowa — 58.69% (correct)
  • Ohio State beats TCU — 59.38% (correct)

The Model’s Upsets

The model predicted three upsets in the first round, all of which came true:

  • Iowa beats Clemson — 68.83%
  • VCU beats UNC — 60.08%
  • Utah State beats Villanova — 61.39%

The Model’s Worst Misses

  • High Point won against Wisconsin — 24.64%
  • Texas A&M won against Saint Mary’s — 36.83%
  • Texas won against BYU — 26.64%

The Final Score

In total, Eric’s Evil Eye correctly predicted 50/63 (79.3%)12 possible picks in the bracket, allowing it to rise to the 99.4th percentile of all brackets made on ESPN this year. The model had three of the correct Final Four members: Illinois, Arizona, and Michigan. The remaining member was Duke, who lost in a stunning, improbable fashion to UConn, although I could have told you Duke would be upset earlier than expected before coding a single thing. Investigating what made the model tick, I had it report which features it concluded to be the most important ones for determining the winner of a given game. As shown in Fig. 2, the three most important determining factors of what makes teams win in March are: kenpom adjusted offensive efficiency, kenpom adjusted defensive efficiency, and seed number13. Apparently not as important to the model are the active coaching length index, 3 point field goal attempt rate, and opponent block percentage. Therefore, this model confirms prior studies quoting kenpom statistics as the quick and simple gold standard for predictive accuracy in March14, and confirms my mom’s strategy of straying away from upsets.

Final Conclusion

For any fan of basketball, March Madness is the epitome of emotional rush. I experienced such a moment on April 4th, 2026, as the champion fighters of Eric’s Golden Mean and Eric’s Evil Eye faced off in a brutally anticipated Final Four game: Arizona versus Michigan. I went into this experiment hoping that basketball is not just an analytical game when it matters the most– that Arizona would prevail because I saw them dominate all regular season with my own eyes, and that heart wins over whatever the heck a forest algorithm is. That being said, when Michigan thumped Arizona essentially from the start, getting out to a 10-1 lead in the first three minutes, I couldn’t help but feel a deep sense of gratification and gratitude for the effort I put in on my code. Eric’s Golden Mean plummeted in my family’s bracket pool standings, yet I could hardly be seen without my Yaxel Lendeborg jersey from then on. In a single game elimination basketball tournament with 68 teams15, truly anything can happen. This project reminds me that you can create a nice image in your head of exactly how a game, or tournament, will play out, yet your one scenario will, statistically speaking, be out-maneuvered by intelligence propagated on years of historical data. Watching Yaxel literally put BTA in celebration with a NCAA Championship hat on his head, I leave feeling inspired to continue coding projects which highlight the heart that Michigan was not-so-secretly showing all year long. Next year, I’ll make sure my bracket is aligned in my newfound ideals:

  Eric's Golden Eye

Feature Descriptions

All statistics listed below were obtained from Jonathan Pilafas’s Kaggle page, “March Madness Historical DataSet (2002 to 2026)” on March 17th, 2026. Therefore, stats in the 2026 season correspond to regular season stats only. Unless otherwise specified, all stats reported here are team-level stats, counted by all player contributions on the team within the given season. The original data source for all stats listed below is kenpom.com.

Adjusted Offensive Efficiency — AdjO

Offensive Efficiency measures the points a team scores per 100 possessions across the season. This stat has been adjusted by Pomeroy to adjust for the strength of opponents played in the season so that AdjO can be compared directly between all D1 teams.

Adjusted Defensive Efficiency — AdjD

Defensive Efficiency measures the points a team concedes per 100 possessions across the season. This stat has been adjusted by Pomeroy to adjust for the strength of opponents played in the season so that AdjD can be compared directly between all D1 teams.

Adjusted Tempo — AdjTempo

Tempo measures the possessions a team has per 40 minutes across the season. This stat has been adjusted by Pomeroy to adjust for the tempo of opponents played in the season so that AdjD can be compared directly between all D1 teams.

FG2Pct

The percentage of field goals a team successfully makes from within the arc, equivalent to a 2-point bucket.

FG3Pct

The percentage of field goals made from outside the arc, equivalent to a 3-point bucket.

FTPct

The percentage of free throws a team makes.

BlockPct

The percentage of opposing team 2-point field goal attempts that are blocked by the pertinent team.

StlRate

The percentage of opponent possessions that end in a steal by the pertinent team.

FG3Rate

The percentage of possessions during which a team attempts a 3 point field goal.

OppFG2Pct

The percentage of 2 point field goals opponents make against a team.

OppFG3Pct

The percentage of 3 point field goals opponents make against a team.

OppBlockPct

The percentage of possessions where a team is blocked by the opposition on a shot attempt.

OppStlRate

The percentage of possessions where a team has the ball stolen by the opposition.

OppFG3Rate

The percentage of 3 point field goals that are made by opposing teams against the pertinent team.

Experience

An estimate of the average number of Division I basketball seasons played by a roster, weighted by minutes played.

Bench

An estimate of the percentage of a team’s total minutes played by non-starters, reflecting roster depth and rotation usage.

Active Coaching Length Index

A measure of the tenure and continuity of the current head coach of a team, indexed relative to other head coaches.

Seed

The assigned NCAA Tournament Seed for a team going into March Madness. Lower numbered seeds reflect stronger teams as determined by the March Madness Selection Committee and they range 1-16.

ORPct

Offensive Rebound Percentage, representing the percentage of available offensive rebounds a team secures after missed shots.
